II. 
Purpose of Testimony and Overview of Filing 
1 
Q. 
What is the purpose of the Panel’s testimony? 
2 
A. 
The purpose of the Panel’s testimony is to support KEDNY’s request to 
3 
increase its gas delivery rates.  In support of this request, the Panel will: 
4 
(i) 
present KEDNY’s historic and forecast financial data for various 
5 
periods in a manner consistent with the Commission’s regulations and 
6 
policies; 
7 
(ii) 
describe KEDNY’s forecast of operation and maintenance (“O&M”) 
8 
expenses, as well as adjustments to those expenses that were made to 
9 
normalize the historic test year amounts; 
10 
(iii) 
describe KEDNY’s efforts to reduce its cost of service and detail how 
11 
savings related to specific Company productivity initiatives were 
12 
reflected in the filing; 
13 
(iv) 
discuss the development of KEDNY’s gas rate base; 
14 
(v) 
support KEDNY’s forecast of regulatory deferral balances, including 
15 
the proposal to consolidate inactive accounts; and  
16 
(vi) 
describe proposed treatment for deferrals that the Commission has 
17 
previously adopted, as well as proposed new deferral mechanisms.  
18 
 
19 
The Panel will also describe the Company’s efforts in connection with the 
20 
preparation of this rate filing to review the accuracy of costs in the historic test 
21

year and to appropriately normalize these results for known and measurable 
1 
changes that have occurred or will occur between the end of the historic test 
2 
year and the rate year.

22 
Q. 
What is the historic test year in these proceedings?   
23 
A. 
The historic test year in these proceedings is the twelve months ended 
24 
December 31, 2018 (“Historic Test Year”).  The Historic Test Year data 
25 
consists of the costs recorded on the books of KEDNY, including: (i) costs 
26 
incurred directly by the Company; (ii) costs charged to KEDNY from 
27 
National Grid Service Company and National Grid Engineering & Survey, 
28 
Inc. (collectively, the “Service Company”); and (iii) costs charged to KEDNY 
29 
from other affiliated companies.   
30 
 
31 


--- Page 13 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 10 of 123 
Q. 
What Historic Test Year and Rate Year information is the Company 
1 
presenting? 
2 
A. 
The Company is presenting operating results for the Historic Test Year and 
3 
forecast data for the rate year, which is the twelve months ending March 31, 
4 
2021 (“Rate Year”).  In addition, the Company is including forecast data for 
5 
the twelve months ending March 31, 2022 (“Data Year 1”), March 31, 2023 
6 
(“Data Year 2”), and March 31, 2024 (“Data Year 3”) (collectively, the “Data 
7 
Years”) for informational purposes and to facilitate the possibility of a multi-
8 
year rate settlement in these proceedings.  The forecast data provides the basis 
9 
for computing the revenue requirement for the Rate Year and Data Years in 
10 
these proceedings.  The information presented in these filings is consistent 
11 
with that required under the Commission’s “Statement of Policy on Test 
12 
Periods in Major Rate Proceedings.” 
13 
 
14 
Q. 
What are KEDNY’s revenue requirements and associated revenue 
15 
deficiencies based on current rates? 
16 
A. 
Based on the cost of service set forth in the Company’s filing, for the Rate 
17 
Year, KEDNY’s revenue deficiency is $236.8 million, based on a 9.65 percent 
18 
return on equity and a 48 percent common equity ratio, as supported by 
19 
Company Witnesses Ann E. Bulkley and Jonathan Cohen.  If a four-year 
20 
settlement is reached, the Company proposes that a return on equity of 10.15 
21 


--- Page 14 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 11 of 123 
percent be used to calculate the revenue requirement, as supported by Ms. 
1 
Bulkley, and that the equity component of the capital structure be increased to 
2 
49 percent in Data Year 1 and 50 percent in Data Years 2 and 3, as supported 
3 
by Mr. Cohen.   
4 
 
5 
Q. 
How does KEDNY propose to address the current revenue deficiencies? 
6 
A. 
The Company is proposing to reset base delivery rates, which were last set in 
7 
the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases, to permit the Company to recover 
8 
its costs of providing service and allow the Company an opportunity to earn a 
9 
fair return.  As part of a multi-year settlement, the Company would consider 
10 
levelizing the proposed rate increase to ease the impact on customers.   
11 
 
12 
Q.   
Does the Company’s proposed revenue increase reflect the impact of 
13 
levelization in the current rate plan? 
14 
A. 
Yes.   The Joint Proposal in the 2016 KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases was the 
15 
result of a concerted effort by Staff, the Companies, and other parties to 
16 
carefully craft a rate plan that levelized the rate increase on an equal 
17 
percentage basis over the three years of the plan.  This approach balanced the 
18 
interest of customers with the need to maintain safe and reliable service.  
19 
Levelization was accomplished by under-recovering revenue requirements in 
20 
the initial year of the rate plan, and over-recovering in the last year.  As a 
21 


--- Page 15 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 12 of 123 
result, KEDNY's current rates for calendar year 2019 generate levelized 
1 
revenues of approximately $108 million.  Starting January 1, 2020, the end of 
2 
the current rate plan, these levelized revenues will be deferred for future 
3 
disposition until the earlier of June 30, 2020 or the date that new rates become 
4 
effective. 
5 
 
6 
The proposed revenue increases in these rate filings build off KEDNY’s 
7 
calendar year 2019 revenues, including the revenues associated with 
8 
levelization.  The Company believes this approach appropriately presents the 
9 
proposed revenue increases in comparison to the rates that customers are 
10 
currently paying and the revenues that those rates are currently providing.  
11 
The Company believes that this approach minimizes customer confusion 
12 
without adversely affecting the ability of the Commission, Staff, or any other 
13 
party to review the Company’s rate increase proposal.  
14

III. 
Historic Test Year Cost Review and Trend Analysis 
1 
Q. 
What efforts did the Company undertake to ensure the accuracy of its 
2 
Historic Test Year costs?  
3 
A. 
The Company recognizes the importance of demonstrating the accuracy of its 
4 
Historic Test Year costs.  Accordingly, to validate the accuracy and integrity 
5 
of Historic Test Year costs, and to facilitate Staff’s review of these costs, the 
6 
Company undertook extensive efforts to ensure that costs incurred in the 
7 
Historic Test Year were thoroughly reviewed and appropriately normalized.   
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Did the Company’s review of Historic Test Year transactions follow the 
10 
same general process as the reviews conducted in prior National Grid 
11 
rate cases? 
12 
A. 
Yes.  The Company followed the same general process undertaken in the 2016 
13 
KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases and the 2017 NMPC Rate Case.  For vendor 
14 
costs, the Company enhanced the testing process for the last two quarters of 
15 
the Historic Test Year, as explained below.   
16 
 
17 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s review of Historic Test Year costs. 
18 
A. 
The Historic Test Year includes (i) costs charged to the Company (direct or 
19 
allocated) from the Service Company and (ii) costs either originating in the 
20 
Company or charged to it by its affiliates.  The Company reviewed costs in 
21

1 
appropriately charged to KEDNY and to provide the Company with additional

Year Review”).   
4

Q. 
Please describe the approach taken by the Company to conduct the 
1 
Historic Test Year Review. 
2 
A. 
The review was focused on testing that costs were appropriately charged to 
3 
the Company, including those allocated from the Service Company, and 
4 
reflected the actual costs incurred to deliver service during the Historic Test 
5 
Year.  The review was designed to identify errors, positive or negative, that 
6 
may have occurred.  
7 
 
8 
The Company reviewed four types of charges: (i) vendor costs; (ii) labor 
9 
costs; (iii) employee expense costs; and (iv) manual general ledger journal 
10 
entries.  For those charges reviewed, the Company reviewed supporting 
11

Vendor Costs 
4 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s review of vendor costs. 
5 
A. 
For each of the first two quarters of the Historic Test Year, the Company 
6 
selected and tested charges for: 
7 
• the top 25 vendors based on dollars approved for payment; 
8 
• 15 sampled vendors selected without bias ranked between 26 and 100 
9 
based on dollars approved for payment; and  
10 
• 10 sampled vendors selected without bias ranked greater than 100 based 
11 
on dollars approved for payment.   
12 
For the third and fourth quarters of the Historic Test Year, the Company 
13 
enhanced the process.  Instead of sampling vendors based solely on dollar 
14 
amounts (and then testing a high percentage of their invoices, no matter how 
15 
small), the Company moved to a risk-based approach that enabled testing of a 
16 
greater number of vendors and unique transactions.  This approach allowed 
17 
the Company to test transactions from vendors who may not be routinely used 
18 
by the Company and therefore may not have been picked up in the volume-
19 


--- Page 23 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 20 of 123 
based sample because their costs were outside the threshold.  Under this 
1 
method, the Company: 
2 
• Examined 40 percent of each unique transaction per vendor and a 
3 
minimum of 10 percent of the invoices per unique transaction.  A 
4 
“transaction” was defined as a vendor’s work on a particular project, 
5 
within a particular department at National Grid.  For example, if a vendor 
6 
was handling ten different projects for one department, each project was 
7 
considered a unique transaction (of which the Company would obtain 40 
8 
percent coverage, i.e., four projects). A minimum of 10 percent of the 
9 
invoices for each of the transactions selected for testing were also 
10 
examined.   
11 
• For Service Company, the same approach was adopted for all vendors 
12 
with aggregate costs of more than $0.100 million (roughly 96 percent of 
13 
the population). 
14 
• Service Company vendors with aggregate costs of less than $0.100 million 
15 
were subject to additional sampling.   
16 
 
17 
As part of the Examination Process, the Company compared the costs 
18 
recorded in the general ledger to the supporting documentation, tested that the 
19 
services related to the company to which they were charged and, for charges 
20

assigned to capital projects, tested that the service was performed in support

of the capital program.

Trend Analysis 
1 
Q. 
Did the Company compare Historic Test Year O&M costs with prior 
2 
period costs?   
3 
A. 
Yes.  The Company performed an analysis to look at changes in expenses 
4 
incurred by the Company from calendar year (“CY”) 2015 through the 
5 
Historic Test Year.  The purpose of the review was to look at trends in costs 
6 
by functional area incurred by the Company directly, as well as from the 
7 
Service Company and affiliates that charge the Company.  Over the past few 
8 
years, there have been a number of changes in the organizational structure of 
9 
the service companies that render it impossible to analyze changes in the costs 
10 
charged to the Company by examining only the overall level of Service 
11 
Company costs charged to the Company from year to year.  Because of these 
12 
organizational changes, the Company’s costs must be examined on a total 
13 
basis to draw meaningful conclusions regarding year-over-year variations.  
14 
This examination was accomplished by combining (i) costs incurred directly 
15 
by the Company, (ii) costs charged to the Company from the Service 
16 
Company, and (iii) costs charged to the Company from other affiliates.   
17 
 
18 
 
The analysis of costs based on the combination of direct and indirect charges 
19 
provides improved clarity on the factors driving cost increases and decreases 
20 
by removing the impact of organizational changes that merely result in shifts 
21 


--- Page 31 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 28 of 123 
rather than absolute changes in costs from year to year.  Overall, the trend 
1 
analysis shows that the total costs for KEDNY increased during the period 
2 
CY15-CY18 due to increases in operational workload, new regulations and 
3 
laws such as incremental paving requirements, and initiatives to modernize 
4 
the Company’s gas and IT systems such as the Gas Business Enablement 
5 
Program (“GBE Program”).  Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 presents a 
6 
comparison of total O&M costs from CY15 to the Historic Test Year.   
 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
What does Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 show? 
9 
A. 
The analysis presented on Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 shows that, over 
10 
the period 2015 through December 31, 2018, the total O&M costs incurred by 
11 
KEDNY increased from $401.3 million to $614.6 million, an increase of 
12 
$213.2 million.  This increase was primarily driven by Gas Business Unit 
13 
costs (increased $137.8 million), which is the function that operates and 
14 
maintains the Company’s gas network.  The increase in costs generally relates 
15 
to work that was included in the Company’s last rate case such as leak prone 
16 
pipe replacement and new safety and compliance initiatives, along with new 
17 
regulatory programs such as inside service line inspections.  Other areas 
18 
responsible for the increase were SIR costs (increased $43.2 million), 
19 
regulatory assessments (increased $10.3 million), IT departmental costs 
20 
(increased $10.1 million), and pension/other post-employment benefits 
21 


--- Page 32 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 29 of 123 
(increased $11.3 million).  Offsetting the increases were decreases to demand-
1 
side management (decreased $14.5 million) and other areas.   
2 
 
 
3 
 
Regarding the source of the cost changes from CY15 to the Historic Test 
4 
Year, Exhibit __ (RRP-2), Schedule 4 illustrates that increased costs over the 
5 
CY15 through Historic Test Year period are attributable to costs directly 
6 
incurred at the Company (an increase of $181.7 million) as well as costs 
7

10 
Q. 
How does the Company determine that the costs it incurs from the 
11 
Service Company are reasonable? 
12 
A. 
The Service Company provides services to the U.S. operating companies, 
13 
including KEDNY, pursuant to the terms of service agreements that are filed 
14 
with the Commission.  The service agreements set forth the services provided 
15 
and charges for those services (i.e., services are provided at actual cost).  The 
16 
services include corporate affairs, customer, environmental, executive and 
17 
administrative, financial, human resources, IT, legal and regulatory, operating, 
18 
strategic planning and corporate performance, gas supply, and energy 
19 
procurement and marketing.   
20 
 
21 


--- Page 33 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 30 of 123 
The Service Company structure positions the Company to (i) attain the 
1 
benefits of economies of scale and scope available from the provision of 
2 
centralized services to a number of operating entities in a manner that ensures 
3 
that no operating entity is cross-subsidizing another, (ii) improve service 
4 
quality throughout the National Grid organization as a result of the enhanced 
5 
job differentiation and specialization that results from the provision of 
6 
services on a centralized basis to a number of operating entities, (iii) improve 
7 
reliability of services provided within the organization, and (iv) implement 
8 
enhanced controls and uniformity of methods and practices throughout the 
9 
National Grid U.S. business. 
10 
 
11 
National Grid has created a process to provide the Jurisdictional Presidents 
12 
and their leadership teams with detailed information concerning all costs 
13 
charged to the operating entities through the service companies.  This 
14 
information provides jurisdictional leadership with regular opportunities to 
15 
challenge and question Service Company charges.  Under National Grid’s 
16 
jurisdictional model, the jurisdictional leadership teams have the key role of 
17 
assuring that customers are receiving appropriate treatment from affiliates in 
18 
terms of service quality and costs.  Service level agreements (“SLAs”) have 
19 
been established between the jurisdictions and the Service Company functions 
20 
to provide a management framework.  The SLAs have been refined, 
21 


--- Page 34 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 31 of 123 
improved, and expanded over the years in accordance with the Niagara 
1 
Mohawk Joint Proposal adopted in Cases 12-E-0201 and 12-G-0202, and 
2 
based on recommendations in the Overland Consulting audit of Service 
3 
Company transactions (Case 10-M-0451), and the Company’s recent gas 
4 
management audit (Case 13-G-0009).  National Grid implemented a 
5 
governance framework for the SLAs that includes monthly meetings to 
6 
discuss budget and/or metric performance.  During these meetings, 
7 
performance issues are addressed or escalated for further review.

IV. 
O&M Expenses 
10 
Q. 
Please explain the methodology for developing the forecast of O&M 
11 
expenses in the Rate Year and Data Years. 
12 
A. 
To develop the O&M forecasts, the Company began by determining the costs 
13 
incurred in the Historic Test Year for the various expense types.  Next, the 
14 
Company reviewed Historic Test Year charges to determine whether specific 
15 
costs should be normalized, for example, as out-of-period or one-time 
16 
charges.  The inflation factors set forth in Exhibit __ (RRP-8) were then 
17 
applied to the majority of expense types to forecast the Rate Year and Data 
18 
Years.  Forecasts of certain expenses were developed using a more 
19 
comprehensive methodology than adjusting for inflation.  For example, labor 
20 
expense was developed by annualizing the monthly and weekly employees on 
21 


--- Page 35 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 32 of 123 
payroll as of the end of the Historic Test Year, adjusting for known changes to 
1 
the employee headcount, and applying contractual and projected wage 
2 
increases to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years.  Additionally, the 
3 
Company adjusted forecast O&M expenses to reflect incremental work 
4 
projected for the Rate Year or costs associated with new initiatives.   
5 
 
6 
Q. 
What assumptions did the Company make regarding non-labor inflation? 
7 
A. 
Except where specifically identified otherwise, the Company applied the non-
8 
labor inflation factor of 4.870 percent to all non-labor expenses in the Historic 
9 
Test Year to forecast the Rate Year.  This factor is equivalent to a 2.6444 
10 
percent average annual increase between the Historic Test Year and the Rate 
11 
Year.  The Company applied the non-labor inflation factor of 2.0355 percent 
12 
to forecast Data Year 1, 1.9895 percent to forecast Data Year 2, and 1.9247 
13 
percent to forecast Data Year 3.  These factors represent the forecast change in 
14 
the GDP Chained Price Index obtained from Moody’s, as provided in Exhibit 
15 
___ (RRP-8).  The Panel addresses calculation of the non-labor inflation 
16 
factor later in its testimony.   
17 
 
18 
 
19

Q. 
Please explain the derivation of the Provider Company O&M expense on 
1 
Pages 1 through 4 of each Schedule of Exhibit ___ (RRP-3). 
2 
A. 
There are several National Grid entities that provide services directly and 
3

4 
directly charged to KEDNY or allocated among the various National Grid 
5 
affiliates (including KEDNY) that receive the services.  For example, when 
6 
the Service Company performs a service for the benefit of a single company, 
7 
that company is directly charged for that service.  If the service is for the 
8 
benefit of multiple companies, however, the charge is allocated to those 
9 
companies using an appropriate allocator.  Pages 1 through 3 detail charges to 
10 
KEDNY from the Provider Companies, including the Service Company.

Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 36 of 123 
Q. 
Please describe how the Service Company charged KEDNY for services 
1 
during the Historic Test Year. 
2 
A. 
Service Company charges were either directly charged to KEDNY or, when a 
3 
service was performed for multiple affiliates, charges were aggregated and 
4 
allocated to all affiliates that benefited from the service using approved 
5 
allocation methodologies.  These allocations have been developed to 
6 
accommodate the different types of costs that are charged by the Service 
7 
Company.  
8 
 
9 
 
The allocators are based on cost causation principles and are designed to 
10 
maximize use of direct allocation codes where charges have been incurred for 
11 
the direct benefit of a single company.  When it is not appropriate to use a 
12 
direct allocation code, a cost causative code is assigned based on the 
13 
appropriate causation driver.  Where it is not appropriate to use a direct or cost 
14 
causative code, then a general allocator is used.  The general allocator used by 
15 
the Service Company is based on a three-point model using Net Margin, Net 
16 
Plant, and Net O&M expense.  These allocation principles are set forth in 
17 
National Grid’s Cost Allocation Manual.

Q. 
How were expatriate costs charged to the Company in the Historic Test 
8 
Year? 
9 
A.  
Costs for expatriate labor and benefits are initially booked at National Grid 
10 
plc.  An analysis is then performed to determine whether the costs are 
11 
recoverable from customers.  Recoverable expatriate costs are compared to 
12 
the current available Market Reference Point (“MRP”) for comparable 
13 
positions.  The lower of the actual cost or MRP is subsequently recorded to 
14 
the Service Company and assessed to the Company and/or other affected 
15 
operating companies.  Accordingly, as costs were reviewed and adjusted 
16 
before being charged to the Company, no adjustments were made for 
17 
expatriate costs in the Historic Test Year.

Q. 
Please describe 53rd week labor costs. 
7 
A. 
Every five years there is an additional, or 53rd, pay week.  Therefore, an 
8 
amount equal to one-fifth of the weekly cost (i.e., one day) is added to the 
9 
labor cost to reflect the normalized cost of the 53rd week.  Fifty-third week 
10 
labor costs are associated with any employee who is paid weekly.  Typically, 
11 
these are represented employees.  The 53rd week labor costs are added to the 
12 
total Rate Year represented labor costs found on Pages 10 through 13 of 
13 
Schedule 23.   
14 
 
15 
Q. 
How were 53rd week labor costs calculated? 
16 
A. 
53rd week labor costs were calculated by taking the estimated annual Rate 
17 
Year labor costs for weekly paid employees divided by 2,080 hours and 
18 
multiplied by eight hours.  The 2,080 hours represents the total number of 
19 
hours worked in a normal calendar year and the eight hours represents the 
20 
normal work hours in a day (i.e., one-fifth of the week).  The calculation was 
21 


--- Page 67 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 64 of 123 
performed by salary band for full time represented employees and part time 
1 
represented employees.

A.

1

Q. 
How did the Company develop the forecast for transportation lease

9 
A.

10

11

12 
added the forecast of lease expense associated with replacement vehicles 
13

14 
general, vehicles become eligible for replacement when fully amortized.  
15 
Third, the Company increased the number of vehicles in fleet inventory to 
16 
support the level of work the Company plans to deliver in the Rate Year.  
17

18 
from sales of replaced vehicles at auction.

Q. 
Please explain how transportation lease expense is calculated. 
21 


--- Page 69 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 66 of 123 
A. 
Estimated delivery dates are established for the replacement and additional 
1 
vehicles along with projected acquisition costs.  Lease expenses are then 
2 
calculated using the acquisition cost, term of the lease, and projected interest 
3 
rate provided by the leasing company.   
4 
 
5 
Q. 
Why did the Company not simply adjust the Historic Test Year for 
6 
inflation to forecast the Rate Year and Data Years? 
7 
A. 
The Company does not believe that adjusting for inflation provides an 
8 
accurate projection of activity in the Rate Year and Data Years.  
9 
Transportation lease expense is impacted by changes in the Company’s fleet.  
10 
Specifically, increases or decreases in lease expense result from vehicles 
11 
being removed, replaced, or added to the Company’s fleet.  In addition, the 
12 
Company’s fleet is comprised of many different types of vehicles and 
13 
equipment.  These vehicles vary in costs and lease terms.  The Company’s 
14 
forecast takes into account these known and measurable changes and, 
15 
therefore, provides a more accurate and reasonable forecast than simply 
16 
adjusting for inflation.  
17 
 
18

V. 
Efficiency and Productivity Cost Reductions 
6 
Q. 
Please describe National Grid’s efforts to reduce costs. 
7 
A. 
National Grid is committed to continuously identifying opportunities to be 
8 
more efficient and productive for the benefit of customers.  Indeed, the 2016 
9 
KEDNY and KEDLI Rate Cases reflected more than $22 million of 
10 
efficiency savings in each year of the rate plan through a combination of 
11 
traditional productivity and targeted savings initiatives.  In this filing, the 
12 
Company is challenging itself to achieve even greater levels of efficiencies 
13 
through an ambitious effort, known as the Accelerate Program, to identify 
14 
and track process improvements and other initiatives to reduce costs.  As a 
15 
result of the efforts through the Accelerate Program, the Company is 
16 
reflecting approximately $31 million and $12 million of O&M reductions for 
17 
KEDNY and KEDLI, respectively, in the Rate Year and each of the Data 
18 
Years, or approximately $124 million and $48 million in efficiencies over 
19 
the four years presented in these filings (excluding inflation).  These savings 
20 
are exclusive of savings associated with the GBE Program, which, while 
21 


--- Page 83 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 80 of 123 
included in the Accelerate Program, have been reflected separately for 
1 
transparency.  These savings are also incremental to the productivity 
2 
adjustment discussed below. 
3 
 
4 
Q. 
Please describe the Accelerate Program. 
5 
A. 
In FY 2019, National Grid announced an ambitious, three-year efficiency 
6 
challenge, called the Accelerate Program, that set out an aspirational target 
7 
of a 20 percent efficiency improvement in O&M and capital expenses across 
8 
the U.S. business by FY 2021.  The Accelerate Program is aimed at 
9 
improving both the quality and cost-effectiveness of National Grid’s services 
10 
to customers. 
11 
 
12 
National Grid purposefully set an ambitious target in the interest of driving 
13 
maximum customer value, and it is uncertain whether this level of 
14 
efficiencies can be achieved.  The Commission has traditionally imputed a 
15 
productivity adjustment of one percent of labor expenses, and even that level 
16 
of efficiencies can be challenging to achieve in a mature business.  
17 
Accordingly, the Company recognized it was setting a very ambitious target 
18 
to achieve reductions this extensive in such a short period of time.  Indeed, 
19 
the Company has identified many initiatives that contribute toward its 
20 
efficiency target (discussed below) but has not identified the means by which 
21 


--- Page 84 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 81 of 123 
to achieve the aspirational 20 percent efficiency reduction across the U.S. 
1 
business.   
2 
 
3 
Q. 
Why did the Company undertake this initiative? 
4 
A. 
Affordability is a significant concern for our customers.  At the same time, 
5 
we need to make investments to modernize the system and implement new 
6 
programs and technologies to meet the changing energy landscape.  These 
7 
include investments to replace our outdated Customer Information System, 
8 
modernize the gas network, implement new digital solutions, and enable 
9 
renewable energy sources.  The need for these investments must be balanced 
10 
against the financial impacts on customers. To address these competing 
11 
concerns, National Grid launched the Accelerate Program.  The Accelerate 
12 
Program is National Grid’s effort to identify efficiencies to enable ongoing 
13 
critical investments and support the State’s long-term policy and 
14 
sustainability objectives, while mitigating customers’ energy costs in a 
15 
manner that maintains affordability.  
16 
 
17 
Q. 
How is National Grid attempting to achieve its efficiency target? 
18 
A. 
National Grid is undertaking a variety of initiatives across its U.S. operations 
19 
that seek to standardize processes and reduce costs.  Example initiatives 
20 
include programs that: 
21 


--- Page 85 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 82 of 123 
• Reduce property tax expense; 
1 
• Deliver capital projects more efficiently; 
2 
• Optimize office space;  
3 
• Reduce contractor and consultant costs; 
4 
• Reduce material and fleet costs; and 
5 
• Utilize tools and technology to drive efficiencies. 
6 
 
7 
All of the Accelerate initiatives are being tracked in a web-based tool, known 
8 
as Wave.  Wave contains various implementation levels, through which 
9 
initiatives must progress before a determination is made that the initiative 
10 
can be counted toward the targets.  A centralized repository for identifying 
11 
and tracking the progress of various Accelerate initiatives provides 
12 
transparency on the progress against targets and avoids overlap.   
13 
 
14 
Q. 
Please explain the implementation levels used to track progress in the 
15 
Wave tool.   
16 
A. 
Each Accelerate initiative is placed at an implementation level (“IL”) based 
17 
on its stage of development, from purely an idea (IL 0) to fully implemented 
18 
(IL 5).  ILs 0 through 2 cover the stages of idea formulation to an initial 
19 
estimate of potential benefits.  In these stages, teams brainstorm initiatives to 
20 
be evaluated as opportunities to deliver process improvements, assigning a 
21 


--- Page 86 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 83 of 123 
rough estimate of the potential benefit as an initial proxy until better 
1 
information is developed to quantify the benefit.  Teams are encouraged to 
2 
include as many ideas as possible.  As such, many initiatives do not move 
3 
beyond IL 2.  The potential benefit becomes more refined when an initiative 
4 
advances to IL 3, where Finance validates that the initiative has the potential 
5 
to deliver savings, and the business puts together a plan to implement the 
6 
initiative.  An IL 3 benefit is still aspirational, however, as the initiative may 
7 
not be implemented for a variety of reasons.  For example, an initiative could 
8 
require a new contract to be negotiated with a vendor or the implementation 
9 
of a new IT solution; without the new contract or IT solution, the feasibility 
10 
or economics of the initiative may be impacted.  Similarly, in the process of 
11 
implementing the initiative, the business could realize that assumptions have 
12 
changed and therefore the initiative cannot be implemented. 
13 
 
14 
It is not until IL 4 where an initiative moves from conceptual to deliverable.  
15 
In IL 4, the business has completed all activities required to deliver the 
16 
initiative.  In IL 5, Finance has confirmed that savings have been realized 
17 
and the actual amount of the savings, which could have changed from the 
18 
original estimate.   
19 
 
20 


--- Page 87 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 84 of 123

to customers, namely those in ILs 4 and 5.  Given the conceptual nature of 
5 
the initiatives in ILs 0 through 3, they are not reflected because it is unknown 
6 
whether they will be implemented, and, if they are, the extent to which any 
7 
savings will materialize.

18 
retirements from plant in service.  The composite depreciation rates were 
19 
developed based on depreciable plant balances as of December 31, 2018.

Q.

1

A.

5

8

9

10

11

12 
After the filing of the March 31, 2018 federal income tax return, the Company 
13 
finalized the ADIT rate change.  The Rate Year and Data Years include the 
14 
amortization of excess federal ADIT for the benefit of customers.  This 
15 
amortization reduces the Company’s effective tax rate and mitigates the rate 
16 
increase to customers.

Q. 
Please explain how the annual federal excess ADIT amortization was 
1 
calculated. 
2 
A. 
The Company has split the excess ADIT between protected plant, unprotected 
3 
plant, net operating loss (“NOL”), and unprotected non-plant balances.  The 
4 
split between protected plant and unprotected plant was determined following 
5 
the implementation of a deferred tax module to the tax depreciation system, 
6 
PowerTax.  Protected plant excess ADIT relates to the temporary differences 
7 
between book and tax depreciation methods and lives only.  The IRS 
8 
normalization regulations require the Average Rate Assumption Method 
9 
(“ARAM”) as the proper way to calculate the return of protected excess ADIT 
10 
if the Company has the data available to implement ARAM.  The PowerTax 
11 
system is able to quantify the ARAM amortization for protected plant excess 
12 
ADIT by applying the current book depreciation rates against the tax basis.  
13 
The Company has a forecast of ARAM amortization for the Rate Year and 
14 
Data Years from PowerTax.  This amount is reflected in Exhibit __ (RRP-11), 
15 
Workpapers to Exhibit ___ (RRP-6), Workpaper 2. 
16 
 
17 
 
Unprotected plant excess ADIT is a result of book and tax basis differences 
18 
such as the repair deduction and contributions in aid of construction and other 
19 
plant temporary differences such as the current tax deduction for cost of 
20 
removal spending.  The Company proposes to use an amortization period 
21 


--- Page 101 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 98 of 123 
representing the average remaining book life of the net book value of plant 
1 
assets to return the unprotected balances to customers.  The NOL unfunded 
2 
ADIT is classified as a protected asset as it was the difference between book 
3 
and tax depreciation, including bonus depreciation, that caused the Company 
4 
to be in an NOL position.  There has been no IRS guidance around the 
5 
suggested method to amortize this asset.  The Company is amortizing the

11 
 
12 
Q. 
Please explain the proration adjustment as it relates to the forecast of 
13 
changes in accumulated deferred federal and state income tax.  
14 
A. 
Sections 1.167(1)-1(h)(6) of the federal income tax regulations provide 
15 
requirements for the amount of reserve for deferred income tax that is 
16 
included as a reduction to rate base in a rate filing.  Part (ii) of this subsection 
17 
requires a proration of monthly deferred tax amounts if the rates relate to a 
18 
“future” period.  Proration is not, however, required for a “historic” period.  
19 
“Future” periods are forecast periods after the date rates go into effect.  
20 
“Historic” periods are all periods before the effective date for rates even if the 
21 


--- Page 108 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 105 of 123 
underlying data is an estimate.  In the filing, deferred tax balances are 
1 
projected for each Rate Year.  On the date the new rates go into effect for each 
2 
year, the entire year is a “future” period, so the entire year’s accumulated 
3 
deferred tax movement is subject to proration.  The pro rata portion is 
4 
determined by multiplying the monthly changes in deferred tax by a fraction, 
5 
the numerator being the number of days remaining in the future period as each 
6 
month’s deferred tax changes occurs and the denominator being the total 
7 
number of days in the future period.  Only the ADIT changes for the 
8 
difference between book and tax depreciation is subject to proration. 
9 
 
10 
Q. 
Please explain the change in ADIT related to plant changes. 
11 
A. 
The Company used its tax depreciation system, PowerTax, to forecast the tax 
12 
depreciation on historic plant balances as of March 31, 2018, the fiscal year 
13 
end of the most recently filed federal income tax return.  All additional 
14 
changes in ADIT related to plant are a direct result of forecast plant additions, 
15 
forecast cost of removal, and forecast book depreciation. The Company 
16 
forecast tax deductions related to plant additions in two layers.  The first layer 
17 
was the new plant additions eligible for the repair deduction.  The repair rate 
18 
was applied as a percentage of total capital expenditures.  The percentage was 
19 
an estimate based on a trend analysis of the actual results of the prior three 
20 
fiscal years’ tax return study for capital plant repairs.  The plant tax basis after 
21 


--- Page 109 ---
Testimony of the Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 106 of 123 
the deduction for repairs was then subject to Modified Accelerated Cost 
1 
Recovery System (“MACRS”) depreciation, using a 20-year tax life.  All tax 
2 
plant deductions were compared to book depreciation and federal and state 
3 
ADIT was computed on the temporary difference. 
4 
 
5 
Q. 
Why is bonus depreciation not included in the ADIT forecast? 
6 
A.   
Under the Act, regulated public utilities were generally prohibited from taking 
7 
bonus depreciation deductions on assets placed in service after September 27, 
8 
2017.  This provision was tied to the provision that permitted regulated public 
9 
utilities to be exempt from the interest expense limitations under new section 
10 
163(j).  New proposed regulation 104397-18 was issued in August 2018.  
11 
Because the bonus depreciation rules and interest limitation rules of the Act 
12 
were linked and because the interest limitation rules did not go into effect 
13 
until the first taxable year after December 2017, the Company was able to take 
14 
bonus depreciation on plant placed in service after September 27, 2017 
15 
through the fiscal year end March 31, 2018.  However, the Company 
16 
interprets the proposed regulation as not allowing bonus depreciation after 
17 
March 31, 2018 and there are no bonus depreciation deductions used in the 
18 
computation of plant related ADIT in the Rate Year or the Data Years.  
19 
 
20

18

20 
The Company will leave the entire excess ADIT in the regulatory liability

13

15

16

17 
Economic Analysis.  The inflation adjustment factor is calculated by relating 
18

December 31, 2018) to the average of the forecast GDPIPD in the Rate Year

in Appendix 2.

the full revenue requirement associated with any shortfall between actual

b. 2013 – 2016 Deferrals 
 
 
In 2013, the City/State Construction deferral mechanism was eliminated and KEDNY’s 
capital tracker mechanism was modified to a downward-only net utility plant reconciliation 
mechanism that includes allocated common plant and depreciation expense.2  To the extent that 
KEDNY’s net utility plant, inclusive of allocated common plant and depreciation expense, falls 
below the combined target average net utility plant and depreciation expense revenue 
requirement, KEDNY is required to establish a regulatory liability for the benefit of customers.  
KEDNY is not permitted to establish a regulatory asset for any increase in the revenue 
requirement that results from the actual net utility plant and depreciation expense exceeding the 
targets.  The mechanism was originally established to operate on a cumulative basis over the 
two-year term ending December 31, 2014, but was extended to four years by the Commission.3  
In October 2015, the Commission modified KEDNY’s capital investment plan for 2015 and 
2016, allowing KEDNY to use its deferred credit balance as of December 31, 2014 to offset the 
revenue requirement associated with its increased capital expenditures in 2015 and 2016.4

c. 2017 – 2020 Deferrals 
The Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059 established two capital trackers for KEDNY: (i) 
the City/State Construction Tracker and (ii) the Net Utility Plant and Depreciation Expense 
Reconciliation Mechanism. 
• City/State Construction Tracker – Section 6.2.2 of the Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-
0059 requires that, to the extent that KEDNY’s actual capital spending for City/State 
construction, net of reimbursements, differs from the forecast amount in a Rate Year, 
KEDNY defers the revenue requirement effect (excluding O&M expenses) associated 
with 90 percent of the difference.   
• Net Utility Plant and Depreciation Reconciliation – Pursuant to Section 6.2.1 of the 
Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059, KEDNY implemented a downward only Net 
Utility Plant and Depreciation Expense Reconciliation Mechanism.  Each Rate Year, 
KEDNY reconciles its actual average net utility plant and depreciation expense 
revenue requirement to the target average net utility plant and depreciation expense 
revenue requirement.  The deferred balance is carried forward each Rate Year and 
summed at the end of the third Rate Year.  If at the end of the third Rate Year the 
cumulative balance results in a regulatory liability, the Company defers the revenue 
requirement impact for the benefit of the customers.  If the cumulative balance results 
in a regulatory asset, no deferral is recorded.  In years that incremental Leak Prone 
Pipe replacement costs are recovered through the Gas Safety and Reliability 
Surcharge, the net plant and depreciation components of the Gas Safety and 
Reliability Surcharge for incremental LPP replacement costs are added to the overall 
Net Utility Plant and Depreciation Expense Mechanism target to avoid any double 


--- Page 131 ---
Appendix A 
Testimony of KEDNY Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 4 of 30 
 
recovery.  Similarly, in years the City/State Construction Tracker mechanism applies, 
the net plant and depreciation components of the City/State Construction Tracker will 
adjust the overall Net Utility Plant and Depcreciation Expense Mechanism target to 
avoid any double recovery.  As of January 1, 2020, the Net Utility Plant and 
Depreciation Expense Reconciliation Mechanism will be converted into a two-way 
tracker until the earlier of the approval of new KEDLI rates via a general rate case or 
June 30, 2020.

5. 
Delivery Rate Adjustment 
Basis for the Deferral 
 
Pursuant to the December 2007 Order, KEDNY revised its tariff to incorporate a 
Delivery Rate Surcharge (“DRS”) in December 2007.6  Changes were made to the Customer 
Billing Charge to include the DRS, which went into effect on a temporary basis on January 1, 
2008.  KEDNY’s tariff revisions to memorialize the DRS were permanently approved by the 
Commission in May 2008.7  The revisions included the establishment of the Delivery Rate 
Adjustment (“DRA”) as a separate line item on customer bills.  The DRA consists of the DRS, a 
Weather Normalization Adjustment for applicable heating customers, the incremental State 
Assessment Charge and, where applicable, the Revenue Decoupling Mechanism.  The DRS 
provided for $5 million in annual rate increases beginning in Rate Year One and was ultimately 
designed to collect $25 million by Rate Year Five.  The DRS expired at the end of 2012.

8. 
Environmental Costs 
Basis for the Deferral 
 
Pursuant to JP-2, KEDNY defers for future recovery one hundred percent of actual SIR 
costs, with the exception of the Coney Island and Citizens sites, as discussed below.  Deferred 
SIR costs include the remediation costs associated with KEDNY’s manufactured gas plant sites 
and Superfund sites, including sites where KEDNY is named as a potentially responsible party.  
KEDNY generally recognizes its SIR responsibilities as a liability on its balance sheet as the 
sites are identified and costs are assessed.  The liabilities are reduced as expenditures are made 
to clean up or remediate sites.  The SIR deferral follows the cash expenditures.   
As described in Gas Rates Joint Proposal in Case 06-G-1185, if the total cost of 
investigating and remediating the Coney Island site, plus the cost for investigating the 
Company’s Citizens site, differs from $33.996 million, KEDNY would absorb or retain 10 
percent of the difference, and the balance would be reflected in the Balancing Account as either 
a debit or credit.11   
Pursuant to Section 6.1.4 of the Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059, each Rate Year, 
KEDNY fully reconciles actual SIR expense (inclusive of Gowanus Canal and Newtown Creek 
costs) to the Forecast Rate Allowance.  Any under or over expenditures will be deferred for

In July 2018, KEDNY, KEDLI, and Niagara Mohawk submitted a notice of a revision to 
the Company’s accounting practices with regard to the capitalization of certain costs charged to 
the Administrative and General (“A&G”) category of accounts in the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission’s Uniform System of Accounts.  In late 2018, the Commission accepted the 
Company’s proposal to apply the A&G capitalization adjustment beginning in FY18 and to defer 
the net revenue requirement impact of the capitalization adjustment for the benefit of customers.  
 
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2018 
The actual deferral balance as of December 31, 2018 was a credit of $16.043 million. 
Forecast of Deferrals through March 31, 2020 
 
As of March 31, 2020, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of $18.636 million. 
 
 


--- Page 151 ---
Appendix A 
Testimony of KEDNY Revenue Requirements Panel 
Page 24 of 30 
 
29. 
Excess Reserve-Tax Cuts & Jobs Act 
Basis for the Deferral 
This account includes the revenue requirement impacts of the change in the corporate 
federal income tax rate from 35 percent to 21 percent, the excess accumulated deferred income 
taxes related to the change in the corporate federal income tax rate, and the offsetting impacts of 
the elimination of bonus depreciation.  The Commission’s Order Determining Rate Treatment of 
Tax Changes in Case 17-M-0815 (issued and effective August 9, 2018) accepted the Company’s 
proposal to defer both the pass back of calendar year 2018 tax savings and the amortization of 
excess ADFIT balances, and retain the Calendar Year 2018 deferred amounts for future rate 
mitigation and/or to offset investments. 
 
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2018 
The actual deferral balance as of December 31, 2018 was a credit of $38.219 million. 
Forecast of Deferrals through March 31, 2020 
 
As of March 31, 2020, the forecast deferral balance is a credit of $38.219 million. 
30. 
NY Facilities  
Basis for the Deferral 
Under the Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059, the Company is recovering an estimate of 
NYFS costs in base delivery rates. The Order Regarding New York Facilities System Agreement 
in Case 18-G-0318 (issued and effective October 18, 2018), approved the Company’s request to 
implement a NYFS Surcharge/Surcredit that would allow the Company to refund any over-
recoveries of NYFS costs as compared to the amount reflected in base rates and recover any 
under-recoveries of such costs.

31. 
Levelization Rate Deferral 
 
Basis for Deferral 
 
Under the Joint Proposal in Case 16-G-0059, beginning January 1, 2020 and continuing 
through the earlier of June 30, 2020 or the date which the Company establish new base delivery 
rates, the Company will defer the difference between the levelized rates and the calculated 
revenue requirements for the benefit of customers. 
 
Actual Deferral through December 31, 2018 
The actual deferral balance as of December 31, 2018 was $0.   
 
Forecast of Deferral through March 31, 2020

Executive summary 
In preparation for KEDNY and KEDLI (collectively ‘the Companies’) rate case filing, a detailed and thorough 
review of the test year transactions (“Financial Review”) was performed. 
This document outlines the testing approach and results of the Financial Review of test year transactions incurred 
by the Companies, led by internal resources within the National Grid Finance Team (the “Finance Team”). 
Scope of our examination 
Our examination is designed to cover subject matter that includes transactions recorded by the following 
subsidiaries of the National Grid USA: 

KEDNY

KEDLI

Service Company
For each entity, the Financial Review report comprises of a Summary of Selected Vendor Costs and a Summary of 
Selected Labor Costs, Employee Expense Costs, and Manual Journal Entries for the twelve-month period ended 
December 31, 2018. 
Risk and approach 
The Finance Team performed a sampling and testing approach consistent with the manner performed for prior cases 
filed with the Commission (except where specifically noted otherwise) to address the risks identified in each area of 
testing.  
Our testing approach was designed to mirror that of an external independent audit. Though the Financial Review is 
being performed by National Grid employees and is therefore not fully independent, the test is not being performed 
by those who have operated the related controls nor recorded the related transactions and therefore does have a 
substantial degree of independence from business process owners.  
Results and findings 
Our results and findings are detailed in the Results and Findings section. The findings include amounts of $2.79 
million related to KEDNY (Section “Results and Findings- KEDNY”), $0.54 million related to KEDLI (Section 
“Results and Findings- KEDLI”) and $6.9 million related to Service Company (Section “Results and Findings- 
Service Company”).   
Exhibit______(RRP-2) 
Schedule 2 
Page 3 of 100


--- Page 174 ---
 
Risk and approach 
 
The subject matter included in the Summary of Costs reports was developed as follows: 
 
Vendor costs – Sampling for testing of vendor costs was performed from a list of amounts approved for payment 
to each vendor in each of the four quarters of calendar year 2018.  
 
For the first half of the year tested, the Finance Team selected items for testing that represent the top 25 vendors 
based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, 15 vendors selected without bias that are ranked between 26 
and 100 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, and 10 vendors selected without bias ranked greater 
than 100 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter. All invoices approved from selected vendors were 
tested except in cases where the vendor had over 149 invoices during the three-month period, in which case a sample 
of invoices for the vendor were tested. The subject matter excludes amounts approved for payment related to 
purchased commodity, as these costs generally are not recovered via base delivery rates. This approach is consistent 
with the approach taken in the 2017 Electric and Gas Rate Cases for Niagara Mohawk and the 2016 KEDNY and 
KEDLI Rate Cases.  
 
For the second half of the year tested, the Finance Team enhanced the testing procedures moving to a risk-based 
sampling approach, in an effort to cover a larger number of unique transactions and greater number of vendors. This 
approach is described in further detail within the Notes section for the respective entity. The population was stratified 
as follows: 
 
 
Other than the individual transaction groups identified, testing samples for the remaining vendor population 
were selected to cover approximately 40% of every unique transaction and a minimum of 10% of the 
invoices per unique transaction for both KEDNY, KEDLI, and Service Company vendors whose total 
expenditures were greater than $100 thousand dollars (96% of the population).  A unique transaction was 
defined as a vendor’s work for a particular project with a particular department at National Grid (e.g. If a 
vendor was performing work for one department under ten different projects, they would each be considered 
a unique transaction of which we would obtain 40 percent coverage [i.e. 4 projects].  A minimum of 10 
percent of the number of invoices associated with each of the unique transactions selected for testing would 
also examined). 
 
 
Service Company vendors which aggregated to less than $100 thousand dollars (~4% of the total population) 
would be subject to additional haphazard sampling. 
 
 
Construction related expenditures:  The team will examine all transactions related to work orders from the 
Company’s Work Management System (Maximo) and Paving system (DPMS) and corresponding other 
paving, permits/summons transactions. 
  
 
Labor costs (KEDNY and KEDLI) – The population for testing for labor costs was based on a financial report 
which included base time and overtime pay, but excluded labor-related overhead costs such as social security 
taxes, life insurance, pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and other welfare 
expenses. All base time and overtime pay was selected for inclusion in the subject matter.   
 
Labor costs (Service Company) – The population for testing for labor costs was based on a financial report which 
included base time and overtime pay, but excluded labor-related overhead costs such as social security taxes, life 
insurance, pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and other welfare expenses. Given 
the large volume of transactions, items were selected that represented (i) the 15 largest cost centers and (ii) 25 cost 
Exhibit______(RRP-2) 
Schedule 2 
Page 4 of 100


--- Page 175 ---
centers selected without bias ranked greater than 15, selected from a population consisting of the 15 largest 
operating departments as determined by payroll cost incurred, and 25 departments selected without bias ranked 
greater than 15, based on payroll cost incurred.  
Employee expense costs – The population for testing for employee expense costs was based on a financial report 
of amounts approved for payment in each quarter. Items were selected that represent the top 25 single employee 
claims (“trip reports”) and top 50 purchase credit card (“P-card”) transactions based on dollars approved for 
payment in each quarter, 15 trip reports selected without bias ranked between 26 and 100 based on dollars 
approved for payment in each quarter, 10 trip reports selected without bias ranked greater than 100 based on 
dollars approved for payment in each quarter, and 25 P-card transactions selected without bias ranked greater than 
50 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter. The Summary of Selected Employee Expense Costs 
did not include any expenses submitted for reimbursement by “Band A” employees, defined as senior executives 
of NGUSA, as well as other costs which were excluded following a keyword search. 
General ledger entries – Testing for manual journal entries was based on a financial report all journal entries that 
impacted manual journal accounts. For each system “document type” included in the list, items were identified for 
selection and presentation in the Summary of Selected General Ledger Entries based on dollar value, as detailed in 
the Notes to each of the Summary of Costs reports.

vendor costs are incurred and 
accurate

To test the financial records that 
vendor costs are allocated to the 
correct company 
2. Review the underlying vendor information for details of
goods purchased or services performed and identify whether
the goods or services relate to / benefit the entity to which
they were charged.
To test the financial records that 
costs related to capital programs or 
operating expenses are appropriately 
classified 
3. Review the underlying vendor information for details of
whether goods purchased, or services performed related to a
capital program or not.
Labor 
costs 
To test the financial records that  
labor costs are accurate 
4.Testing employee hourly pay rates with reference to
employee compensation arrangement information.
5.Review monthly payroll totals and identify any outlier
information, obtain explanation for any unusual fluctuations
and test that they are reasonable.
To test the financial records that 
payroll costs are charged to Service 
Company orders consistent with 
work performed (Service Company 
only) 
6.Review amounts charged by employees charging Service

is consistent with the employee’s job title and functional
area.

any unusual fluctuations
To test the financial records that 
labor costs are allocated to the 
correct companies (KEDNY/KEDLI 
only) 
8. Perform analytics by employees and compare with the
average pay rate for each grade to identify and investigate 
any unusual fluctuations.  
9.Review time capture records for all employees over the 12-
month period; metrics obtained were applied to identify
outlier entries (e.g. more than 12 hours in a day, hours
worked between midnight and 4 am, multiple entities
charged in a day, order/region/segment/ company charged
which is inconsistent with the employee’s job title and
functional area). Inquiry procedures were performed to
investigate inconsistencies.

expenses

employee expenses are accurate and 
submitted 
consistent 
with 
the 
Company policy  
10. Obtain the claim information and supporting documents
submitted; compare such documents to the requirements of
the Company policy. Also verify the expenses are allocated
to a reasonable order based on the employee’s job title and
functional area. “Band A” employee expenses and
transactions identified as part of the keyword search were
excluded from this testing.
Journal 
entries

journal

underlying transaction  
11. Obtain copies of the approved journal entry submission

and recalculate elements of the underlying support to test its
accuracy.

Notes to the Summary of Costs- KEDNY and

1.Background 
 
a. KEDNY 
 
The Brooklyn Union Gas Company d/b/a National Grid NY (“KEDNY”) distributes natural gas to retail 
customers in the boroughs of Brooklyn Staten Island and two-thirds of the borough of Queens, all in New York 
City.  
 
KEDNY is a wholly-owned subsidiary of KeySpan Corporation, which is a wholly-owned subsidiary of National 
Grid USA (“NGUSA”).  NGUSA is a public utility holding company with regulated subsidiaries engaged in the 
generation of electricity and the transmission, distribution, and sale of both natural gas and electricity.  NGUSA 
is a direct wholly-owned subsidiary of National Grid North America Inc. (NGNA) and an indirect wholly-owned 
subsidiary of National Grid plc, a public limited company incorporated under the laws of England and Wales. 
 
KEDNY separately issues financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting requirements of 
the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) as set forth in its applicable Uniform System of Accounts 
and published accounting releases (together, the FERC USoA), as well as financial statements prepared in 
accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States (GAAP).  The subject matter 
presented in the Summary of Costs is prepared consistent with the “Basis of Accounting” described in notes 
2 to 5 below, which are not necessarily the same as the accounting requirements of the FERC USoA or GAAP. 
 
b. KEDLI 
 
KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid (“KEDLI”) distributes natural gas to customers in Nassau and 
Suffolk counties in Long Island, New York, and the Rockaway Peninsula in Queens, New York.  
 
KEDLI is a wholly-owned subsidiary of KeySpan Corporation, which is a wholly-owned subsidiary of NGUSA. 
NGUSA is a public utility holding company with regulated subsidiaries engaged in the generation of electricity 
and the transmission, distribution, and sale of both natural gas and electricity.  NGUSA is a direct wholly-owned 
subsidiary of NGNA and an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of National Grid plc, a public limited company 
incorporated under the laws of England and Wales. 
 
KEDLI separately issues financial statements prepared in accordance with the accounting requirements of the 
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) as set forth in its applicable Uniform System of Accounts and 
published accounting releases (together, the FERC USoA), as well as financial statements prepared in accordance 
with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States (GAAP).  The subject matter presented in the 
Summary of Costs is prepared consistent with the “Basis of Accounting” described in notes 2 to 5 below, which 
are not necessarily the same as the accounting requirements of the FERC USoA or GAAP.  
 
2.  Vendor Costs 
 
Summary of Selected Vendor Costs – During each of the quarters in the period from January 1, 2018 to 
December 31, 2018, KEDNY and KEDLI approved payments to third party vendors totaling $937.8 and $284.5 
million, respectively.  The Summary of Selected Vendor Costs represents vendor costs “approved for payment” 
Exhibit______(RRP-2) 
Schedule 2 
Page 45 of 100


--- Page 216 ---
 
during each of the quarters in the period from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2018, related to the selected 
vendors listed. 
 
This subject matter, designed to reflect a component of total vendor costs, was developed as follows.  The Finance 
Team obtained a list of amounts approved for payment by KEDNY and KEDLI (or the “Companies”) to each 
vendor.  For each quarter during the first half of the year, items were selected that represent the top 25 vendors 
based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, 15 vendors selected without bias that are ranked between 
26 and 100 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter, and 10 vendors selected without bias ranked 
greater than 100 based on dollars approved for payment in each quarter.  
 
For each quarter during the second half of the year, the Finance Team enhanced the testing procedures moving to 
a risk-based sampling and testing approach, in an effort to cover a larger number of unique transactions and greater 
number of vendors.  A unique transaction was defined as a vendor’s work for a particular project with a particular 
department at National Grid (i.e. if a vendor was performing work for one department under two projects, they 
would each be considered a unique transaction). 
 
For these periods, the vendor population was stratified by certain significant transaction groups.  When designing 
the testing approach for the individual transaction groups, consideration was given to the broader internal control 
environment.  To this effect, certain significant transaction groups were deemed to be tested 100% of the vendor 
population value, while others were sampled based on the risks identified, to achieve the test objectives. Specifically, 
the population was stratified as follows: 
 
 
Other than the individual transaction groups identified, testing samples for the remaining vendor population 
were selected to cover 40% every unique transaction per vendor and a minimum of 10% of the invoices per 
unique transactions.  A unique transaction was defined as a vendor’s work for a particular project with a 
particular department at National Grid (e.g. If a vendor was performing work for one department under ten 
different projects, they would each be considered a unique transaction of which we would obtain 40 percent 
coverage [i.e. 4 projects].  A minimum of 10 percent of the number of invoices associated with each of the 
unique transactions selected for testing would also examined) 
 
Construction related expenditures:  The team will examine all transactions related to work orders from the 
Company’s Work Management System (Maximo), Paving system (DPMS) and corresponding other paving, 
permits/summons transactions 
 
The subject matter excludes amounts approved for payment related to purchased commodity and storm 
restoration, as these costs generally are not recovered via the Company’s base delivery rates.  
 
To capture and account for vendor costs, the Company initiates work orders under two types of projects, (1) capital 
projects, under which work orders are designed to capture costs incurred in the execution of the Company’s capital 
programs, and (2) expense projects, under which work orders are designed to capture costs incurred in the 
performance of non-capital-related activity.  The subject matter and basis of accounting reflects the initial 
determination of whether the vendor costs were assigned to capital projects or expense projects.  System-generated 
entries (generally related to the allocation of engineering-related work order design adjustments, or the 
apportionment of overhead) and adjustments to allocate elements of work orders assigned to capital projects to 
expense, are not contemplated in the subject matter. 
 
Basis of Accounting – Vendor costs included in the Summary of Selected Vendor Costs for each of the quarters in 
the period from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2018 represent costs “approved for payment” for each named 
vendor during the period presented.  Irrespective of when the goods or services were received, for purposes of this 
presentation, vendor costs are considered approved for payment upon: 
 
- 
internal acknowledgment that the goods or services have been received, and 
- 
payment of the invoice.

All costs included in the Summary of Selected Vendor Costs have been “approved for payment” by the Company, 
and properly allocated and charged to the Company and its affiliates, in accordance with the Company’s Cost 
Allocation Manual.  The Cost Allocation Manual is further described in Note 6.  Note that vendor costs may 
have been incurred before the period from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2018, but if both elements above 
were not present until after January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2018, such costs would consequently be “approved 
for payment” during the period presented and included in the accompanying Summary of Selected Vendor Costs.  
Likewise, vendor costs incurred during the period from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2018, where both 
elements above were not present prior to December 31, 2018, are not considered “approved for payment” during 
the period presented, nor included in the accompanying Summary of Selected Vendor Costs. This accounting 
policy, applied in the Summary of Costs, is a basis of accounting other than GAAP and the FERC USoA. 
 
Upon satisfaction of the conditions approving a cost for payment, the cost is assigned to a work order as 
follows: 
 
- 
Costs incurred in support of the Company’s capital program are assigned to work orders capturing costs under 
capital projects. 
 
- 
Costs related solely to operating activities are assigned to work orders capturing costs under expense 
projects, or internal orders capturing expense items specific to the Company and incurred outside of the 
Company’s capital program. 
 
3. Labor Costs 
 
Summary of Selected Labor Costs – During the period from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2018, 
KEDNY and KEDLI recorded costs to employees of $205.4 and $114.6 million, respectively, in 
consideration for work undertaken for the benefit of the Company. This amount includes base time and 
overtime pay but does not include labor-related overhead costs such as social security taxes, life insurance, 
pensions, post-retirement benefits other than pension, medical, dental and other welfare expenses. All base 
time and overtime pay was selected for inclusion in the subject matter.   
 
Employees of the Company and its affiliates charge time to system work orders, similar to the process 
described above for vendor costs. Labor costs are recorded by the Company’s payroll and time capture 
system. Labor charges to work orders may be made by a direct employee of the Company, or by an employee 
of an affiliate company who is performing work for the benefit of the Company. 
 
Basis of accounting – Amounts presented in the Summary of Selected Labor Costs represent amounts due 
for base time and overtime to employees of the Company or its affiliates for time charged during the period 
presented and have been allocated consistent with the Company’s Cost Allocation Manual. Amounts 
presented in the Summary of Selected Labor Costs have been charged to capital and operating cost line items 
within the general ledger in a manner consistent with the nature of the work performed.

incurred totaling $2.1 and $1.2 million, respectively. Business expenses are approved for payment if they 
are incurred in the normal course of business, in accordance with the Company’s internal policies, and 
include business travel, accommodation, spot purchases of goods, and other out-of-pocket expenses.  The 
Summary of Selected Employee Expense Costs includes a subset of such expenses.  This subject matter, 
designed to reflect a component of total employee expense costs, was developed as follows.  The Finance

5. General Ledger Entries 
 
Summary of Selected Manual Journal Entries – During the period from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 
2018, the Company recorded entries to the general ledger via automated journal entry and manual journal 
entry processes.  Entries in the Companyies’ general ledgers are assigned a “document type” (doc type), a 
unique two-digit code, designed to identify the source and nature of the journal entry.  The complete 
population of operating expenses recorded is an aggregation of amounts recorded under all doc types to the 
relevant general ledger accounts.  Costs approved for payment to vendors are recorded in the general ledger 
under doc types KR, RE, RS, and KG; labor costs are recorded under doc type AB; and employee expense 
costs under doc types TR and YU.  Entries recorded under the doc types KP, YV and WE are for the usage 
of materials, the inverse (receipt) of which is recorded initially as a RS or RE entry. 
 
Additional entries to the general ledger to allow the Company to maintain underlying books and records on a 
GAAP and FERC USoA basis are recorded via manual or automated entry under separate doc types.  
 
A list of amounts recorded as operating expense under all doc types, and the items noted below were 
identified for selection and presentation in the Summary of Selected General Ledger Entries.  “Operating 
expense” in this case is defined as the aggregate of amounts recorded to general ledger accounts beginning 
with “C6_”, “U6_“, “C40_”, “U40_”, “C411_” or“U411_”, excluding general ledger account C4000000 
(Operating Revenue), and general ledger accounts related to income taxes.  From this population, the method 
applied to select items for inclusion in the Summary of Selected General Ledger Entries was to select the 
items with the largest dollar net impact for the doc types considered for inclusion in the subject matter (see 
below).  
 
 
Amounts presented as “AB” entries in the Summary of Selected General Ledger Entries are a subset of 
entries recorded for manual adjustments to costs or internal orders for items other than labor costs.  The 
Summary of Selected General Ledger Entries includes the impact of the largest AB entries identified as 
the largest entries impacting the largest general ledger line items (measured by absolute value). 
Amounts related to property tax expense and regulatory amortizations were not included in the 
Summary.
